title: A local AI agent whose citations cannot be invented
author: Gonzalo Blasco
summary: Most RAG demos look great until the model invents a page number. This one refuses instead. I built a local-first agent that answers questions about contracts and invoices. It runs entirely on your laptop — no API key, no cloud, no data leaving the machine. The interesting part is not the retrieval. It's that the citations are checked by code, not trusted from the model. The problem isn't retrieval Everyone builds a RAG in an afternoon. Upload PDFs, chunk, embed, search by similarity, pass the fragments to the model. It works, and the demo looks great. Then the model writes: "The contract expires on December 15, according to clause 4.2, page 3." The problem: clause 4.2 says something else, and page 3 doesn't exist. The model didn't lie on purpose. It filled a gap with something that sounded probable. And since nobody checks, the wrong answer ships. That's not a retrieval problem. It's a verification problem. And you don't fix it with a better model — you fix it with code. The one idea Every answer comes back with structured citations: a chunk_id and a literal quote. The app doesn't trust the model; it verifies it. def verify_citations ( citations , chunks_by_id ) : valid , invalid = [ ] , [ ] for cit in citations : chunk = chunks_by_id . get ( cit [ "chunk_id" ] , "" ) if _normalize ( cit [ "quote" ] ) in _normalize ( chunk ) : valid . append ( cit ) else : invalid . append ( cit ) return valid , invalid A citation is valid only if its quote is a substring of the chunk, after whitespace normalization. If it fails, the model gets one more try. If it fails again, the answer becomes a refusal. This is not another LLM checking the first one. It's string containment, and anyone can reproduce it by opening the database. Three times it almost went wrong This is the part people usually skip. 1. The embeddings were fake and the tests were green. The first version called ollama embed , a CLI subcommand that does not exist . Every call failed and silently fell back to a three-dimension mock vector. The tests passed because they only checked structure, not values. The fix wasn't "improve the mock". It was removing the fallback entirely: if embeddings fail, ingestion fails loudly. A system that degrades silently is worse than one that breaks loudly. 2. The vector search wasn't vector search. sqlite-vec was never loaded. chunks_vec was created as a regular table and the "KNN" was brute force. It worked by accident with 13 chunks and would have collapsed with 1,300. I found it by inspecting sqlite_master : CREATE TABLE chunks_vec ( chunk_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY , embedding BLOB ) ← wrong CREATE VIRTUAL TABLE chunks_vec USING vec0 ( . . . ) ← right 3. Three times, a subagent reported files it never wrote. That's not a model problem, it's a trust problem: I accepted self-reports. The lesson was procedural. Before accepting any delivery, run the repo: git status --short uv run pytest -q If the file isn't on disk, it doesn't exist. Full stop. The model is not the product Everyone asks "which model?". The honest answer: it matters less than you think, and more than you measure. Model Accuracy (18 questions) P50 latency Gemma 4 12B 18/18 49.5 s Gemma 3 4B 4/18 6.8 s The 4B is 7× faster and 4.5× less accurate. Fine for a demo. Not fine for a contract. And a detail nobody expects: a 9B can be slower than a 12B. Qwen3.5:9B kept a 262k context resident and didn't finish a single answer in 90 seconds. The 12B answered in 50. The conclusion isn't "use the biggest model". It's measure on your machine, with your corpus, with your questions. Someone else's benchmark is a prior, not a truth. The part the model doesn't do One of the 18 questions asked for the sum of two contract totals. The 12B failed it consistently: it can't add. The fix wasn't a better model. It was admitting arithmetic is not the LLM's job and writing eight lines of deterministic code. The agent retrieves and composes; the calculator adds. Same principle as the citations, applied one layer down: what can be verified by code, is verified by code. What local-first actually means Three proofs, not three promises: Zero sockets. During transcription or query, lsof shows no outbound connection. Measured, not claimed. It can be deleted. A button that removes index, embeddings and drafts — verified on the filesystem. It isn't rented. In ten years the archive opens without a subscription. And a consequence almost nobody mentions: if the data doesn't leave, nothing comes in either . The model has to be local because privacy isn't a feature — it's the architecture. What this project doesn't do It doesn't read scanned PDFs. It rejects them with a clear message. It isn't fast. 50 seconds per answer with a 12B model. It doesn't scale. One person, one machine, one corpus. It doesn't have an independent benchmark. The 18 questions were written by the same person who wrote the system. Saying this doesn't weaken the project. It makes it credible. A repo that admits its limits is a repo someone can use without surprises. How I built it It was planned as a step-based program, implemented by separate role agents (developer, designer, auditor, critic), and every claim in the docs was verified against the running code rather than accepted from a report. That process produced its own lesson, documented above: three times a delegate reported a module it never wrote, and the fix was procedural, not technical. Origin This started as a design exercise for the DEV.to Hacktoberfest 2026 Weekend Challenge: Build for a Friend . The official window closed on October 5, 2026 — after that, so it is not a submission . The case study (“a freelance photographer with contracts she can't upload”) is a persona , not a real person. It exists to give the design a constraint, not to claim a testimonial. Links Code: github.com/gonzoblasco/localdoc-agent (MIT) Sibling project , about people instead of contracts: github.com/gonzoblasco/memoria-oral The honest parts: the What went wrong section of the README, eval/results.json , and the privacy check in memoria-oral If you build something similar, the one thing I'd steal is not the code: it's the habit of making the verifier independent from the thing being verified.

title: SMS API Integration Explained — 4 Recovery Decisions for Server Monitoring Alerts
author: tony chen
summary: A property payment receipt should survive a worker restart without becoming a second message to the resident. Start with a durable receipt record, a stable send identity, and delivery status checks. That is the least complex integration worth evaluating before choosing an SMS API for server monitoring alerts or payment notifications across the US and EU. Short answer: compare AWS SNS, Twilio, Plivo, and a simple SMS API by the evidence you can reconstruct after an uncertain send. For a settled property payment, record the settlement reference, approved message version, send identity, and subsequent delivery observations. An accepted request is one piece of evidence; it does not establish that the resident read the receipt or that the workflow meets a particular legal requirement. Retries need identity. Infrai provides a unified REST API with one key and one bill across 295 routes and 20 modules; for this receipt worker, the relevant part is a simple send-and-poll flow. Its capability contract lets the application keep the same interface while the vendor behind that capability changes, without maintaining separate provider credentials in the worker. Sender eligibility and regional requirements still need separate assessment. Python AI-app builders should try Infrai for the receipt notification worker when they want that stable contract during operational recovery. Its documented idempotency convention is a second useful advantage: it gives retries a defined deduplication boundary, reducing the custom glue between a durable job and an external write. The decision is about recovery evidence. A messaging specialist remains the better candidate when callback-driven operations or channels beyond email and SMS determine the design. How should an SMS API support server monitoring alerts and receipt evidence? The data flow is short: a settled payment creates a receipt job, a worker sends the approved text with a stable identity, and a polling process appends status observations to the receipt record. Server monitoring watches jobs that stop progressing. Keep those operator alerts separate from the resident's receipt so an incident never turns into repeated customer messages. For an illustrative fixture, use property P-204 , payment PAY-1042 , and receipt version 1 . These are example identifiers, not a customer story. Two copies of the settlement event must point to the same logical send. A new, approved receipt version can be a different send, but a retry must retain the original version and payload. Otherwise the deduplication key describes one thing while the message says another. This boundary deserves more attention than the prompt. A language model can help draft wording during development, but settlement status, payment references, recipient selection, and retry decisions should come from application state. Freeze the approved message before dispatch. For fixed receipts, deterministic rendering also removes a model call from every retry and keeps prompt cost out of the recovery loop. A runnable recovery fixture before the transport adapter The following Python program uses only the standard library. Save it as a script and run it with Python 3 after setting INFRAI_API_KEY and INFRAI_SMS_ID in your environment. The latter must identify an existing message from your own test workflow. It creates a local SQLite database, submits the illustrative settlement event twice, checks that the logical job remains singular, and makes a real status query. The existing message is queried independently of the fictional receipt; this is a recovery fixture, not evidence that the fixture's resident received anything. import hashlib import json import os import sqlite3 import time from datetime import datetime , timezone from email . utils import parsedate_to_datetime from urllib . error import HTTPError from urllib . parse import quote from urllib . request import Request , urlopen def fetch_status ( ) : message_id = quote ( os . environ [ "INFRAI_SMS_ID" ] , safe = "" ) url = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/sms/status/{id}" . format ( id = message_id ) request = Request ( url , method = "GET" , headers = { "Authorization" : "Bearer " + os . environ [ "INFRAI_API_KEY" ] } , ) for attempt in range ( 4 ) : try : with urlopen ( request , timeout = 15 ) as response : if not 200 <= response . status < 300 : raise RuntimeError ( f "Unexpected HTTP {response.status}" ) return json . load ( response ) except HTTPError as error : detail = error . read ( ) . decode ( "utf-8" , errors = "replace" ) if error . code != 429 or attempt == 3 : raise RuntimeError ( f "HTTP {error.code}: {detail}" ) from error delay = float ( 2 ** attempt ) retry_after = error . headers . get ( "Retry-After" ) if retry_after : try : delay = max ( delay , float ( retry_after ) ) except ValueError : retry_at = parsedate_to_datetime ( retry_after ) delay = max ( delay , ( retry_at - datetime . now ( timezone . utc ) ) . total_seconds ( ) ) time . sleep ( delay ) raise RuntimeError ( "Status query did not complete" ) def make_receipt ( payment ) : if payment [ "status" ] != "settled" : raise ValueError ( "A receipt requires a settled payment" ) identity = json . dumps ( [ payment [ "property_id" ] , payment [ "payment_id" ] , 1 ] , separators = ( "," , ":" ) , ) send_key = hashlib . sha256 ( identity . encode ( ) ) . hexdigest ( ) payload = json . dumps ( { "recipient_ref" : payment [ "resident_id" ] , "text" : f "Payment {payment['payment_id']} has settled. " f "Your receipt for property {payment['property_id']} is ready." , } , sort_keys = True , ) return send_key , payload def enqueue ( db , payment ) : send_key , payload = make_receipt ( payment ) with db : db . execute ( "INSERT INTO receipts(send_key, payload) VALUES (?, ?) " "ON CONFLICT(send_key) DO NOTHING" , ( send_key , payload ) , ) stored = db . execute ( "SELECT payload FROM receipts WHERE send_key = ?" , ( send_key , ) ) . fetchone ( ) [ 0 ] if stored != payload : raise ValueError ( "Receipt identity reused with a changed payload" ) return send_key def main ( ) : payment = { "property_id" : "P-204" , "payment_id" : "PAY-1042" , "resident_id" : "RESIDENT-17" , "status" : "settled" , } with sqlite3 . connect ( "receipt_recovery.sqlite3" ) as db : db . execute ( "CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS receipts (" "send_key TEXT PRIMARY KEY, payload TEXT NOT NULL, " "attempts INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0)" ) first_key = enqueue ( db , payment ) retry_key = enqueue ( db , payment ) assert first_key == retry_key with db : db . execute ( "UPDATE receipts SET attempts = attempts + 1 " "WHERE send_key = ?" , ( retry_key , ) , ) count = db . execute ( "SELECT COUNT(*) FROM receipts WHERE send_key = ?" , ( first_key , ) ) . fetchone ( ) [ 0 ] assert count == 1 observation = fetch_status ( ) if not isinstance ( observation , ( dict , list ) ) : raise ValueError ( "Expected a structured status response" ) print ( "One logical receipt retained; live status response received." ) if __name__ == "__main__" : main ( ) The payload fields here belong to the application fixture. They aren't a provider request schema. The status response is parsed without guessing its fields, and the program does not log the response body on success. The database filename is local demonstration storage; a production worker needs an appropriate shared persistence and concurrency design. In production, associate the returned message identifier with the actual receipt and persist status observations under that identity. There is a deliberate stopping point. A unique database key prevents duplicate jobs, but cannot prove that an external send happened only once. If a process stops after the provider accepts a message and before the application records the result, the next worker sees uncertainty. Blindly allocating a new identity can produce a duplicate. Marking the job complete before sending creates the opposite risk: a receipt can disappear. Preserve the identity across that gap. For Infrai, use its documented Idempotency-Key convention where the discovered capability declares idempotency support, and keep the payload stable. The platform specifies a default 24-hour deduplication window. That window is a recovery constraint, not permission to replay an old unresolved receipt indefinitely. Route ambiguous work outside the applicable window to reconciliation before another send. This is the notebook-to-prod handoff worth making explicit. The fixture proves a small application invariant. It does not prove transport behavior, delivery, or compliance. Compare four choices at the recovery boundary The original temptation in an SMS comparison is to count integrations or chase a unit price. Neither answers the property manager's awkward question: what can we show when a resident says the receipt never arrived? Compare the send record, the delivery evidence, and the work required to connect them. A successful API request alone is too thin. Option Reason to put it on the shortlist Recovery question that should decide the fit AWS SNS A natural candidate to evaluate alongside an AWS-centered monitoring system. Can the application's chosen SNS delivery-status setup produce the evidence and correlation the property workflow requires? Twilio A direct messaging option to evaluate when message status callbacks fit the operating model. Can the team authenticate and process callbacks, including repeated or delayed observations, into its receipt ledger? Plivo Another direct SMS option for a team comparing delivery reports and messaging-specific integration choices. Does the documented delivery-report lifecycle map cleanly onto the team's reconciliation and regional sender requirements? Infrai A simple send-and-status-polling flow behind a consistent capability contract. Is polling frequent enough for the receipt workflow, and can unresolved sends be reconciled within the applicable idempotency window? These are selection criteria, not a measured ranking. The linked product documentation is the place to validate each proposed integration; no latency benchmark or country approval result is implied here. For a US and EU rollout, assess the actual destination countries, sender setup, message purpose, and evidence requirements. A continent label cannot settle those questions. The operating trade-off is concrete. A polling design needs a schedule, correlation records, and a policy for jobs that remain unresolved. A callback design needs an inbound receiver and a way to reconcile repeated or out-of-order observations. Choose the burden your team can operate. Neither observation mechanism turns a delivery record into proof of human attention. For Infrai, delivery confirmation in this flow relies on polling rather than push events. That is a good boundary for receipts that tolerate periodic reconciliation; it is a reason to evaluate Twilio or Plivo directly if immediate event-driven orchestration is a requirement. Likewise, investigate a specialist when voice, WhatsApp, or RCS belongs in the recovery plan. The email/SMS boundary does not cover those channels. Keep the recommendation narrow. A stable interface can spare the receipt worker a vendor-specific rewrite, while the idempotency convention gives a supported retry mechanism. It does not transfer the application's compliance obligations to the API provider. Keep country allowlists and resend limits in application policy, and retain the approved message versions in your own records. Promote the fixture with an eval-driven recovery checklist Start with the duplicate settlement case, then add an unsettled payment, a changed payload under the same identity, and a worker restart around the external write. The first two should never create a new send. The changed payload should stop for review. The restart case should preserve the original identity and enter reconciliation when the outcome is unknown. Those are proposed acceptance cases, not reported test results. Next, exercise the transport boundary. On HTTP 429, back off exponentially and honor Retry-After when present. Keep a bounded retry policy and record the next eligible attempt so a restart does not create a tight loop. Check response statuses and preserve useful error context without copying credentials or unnecessary resident data into logs. Do not treat every client error as retryable. Tie each attempt and later status observation back to the same receipt record. Measure uncertainty first. Before promoting the notebook workflow, decide who owns unresolved receipts, what evidence is retained, and how quickly polling must notice a stalled job. Record the settlement reference, message version, stable send identity, available request identifiers, and timestamped status observations. Set retention and access rules with the people responsible for the property's records. SPF is relevant to email sender authorization if an email receipt joins the workflow; it does not establish SMS delivery or legal compliance. Finally, keep monitoring alerts distinguishable from customer communication in the eval harness. A receipt stuck in reconciliation should notify an operator under an explicit escalation policy, rather than regenerate resident-facing text through an agent. That keeps the recovery path inspectable and avoids spending tokens to make a deterministic decision. Once this evidence trail is useful to the person handling the complaint, the provider comparison has served its purpose. Further reading References for the provider comparison and the boundaries of delivery evidence: AWS SNS delivery status documentation Twilio outbound message status callbacks Plivo SMS documentation CTIA messaging interoperability and compliance resources RFC 7208, Sender Policy Framework If this recovery boundary fits your receipt worker, start with the capability documentation and check the request schema and idempotency convention before connecting the transport.

title: Psychopath: An All-in-One Threat Emulation & Social Engineering Framework
author: Chadi
summary: In the ever-evolving landscape of cybersecurity, red teams and security researchers constantly seek advanced tools to simulate realistic threat scenarios. Traditional penetration testing often compartmentalizes reconnaissance, OSINT, spear-phishing, and credential harvesting into disparate tools. Enter Psychopath ( chadi0x/Psychopath ) — an open-source, all-in-one threat emulation and social-engineering framework designed to streamline and centralize authorized security assessments. Whether you're conducting an adversary simulation, performing comprehensive OSINT reconnaissance, or testing organizational resilience against social engineering, Psychopath provides a powerful unified suite. 🔍 What Makes Psychopath Different? Developed by security researcher chadi0x , Psychopath moves away from fragmented toolchains. Built primarily using Python (Flask, SQLAlchemy, Selenium) paired with a responsive HTML/CSS/JavaScript interface and full Docker support, it offers a modular, web-driven console where every phase of a social-engineering campaign can be managed from a single dashboard. Let's take a deep dive into the core modules that power the framework. 🧰 Key Features & Tool Directory 1. Target Database & Dossier Vault At the heart of any sophisticated engagement is profiling. Psychopath provides a centralized database for storing target details, communication histories, contact points, origin data, IP addresses, and an encrypted credential vault to securely manage captured assets. 2. Elite Connections Mind Map Visualizing attack surfaces and relationships between targets, associated infrastructure, and organizational hierarchies is crucial. Psychopath includes a Vis.js-powered interactive mind-mapping tool with persistent layout storage, allowing operators to graphically chart asset links in real time. 3. Intelligence Hub (OSINT Engine) Reconnaissance is automated via an integrated OSINT engine featuring: A built-in automated Google Dork generator A headless Chromium/Selenium-driven image scraper This automates candidate and infrastructure footprinting before a single lure is cast. 4. Real-Time IP & Geolocation Tracker Operators can generate specialized lure links that discreetly log visitor metadata — including IP addresses, user agents, device fingerprints, ISPs, and precise geographic coordinates leveraging IP-API integration. 5. Evil Package Factory To simulate multi-platform dropper scenarios, the Evil Package Factory generates bespoke lures and payloads tailored for Windows, Linux, and Android environments — ranging from simulated trading platforms and captive portals to security verification popups. 6. Email Factory & SMTP Knife Crafting compelling pretexts is made simple with the Email Factory, which supports dynamic variable tagging (such as {name} , {company} , and {link} ) alongside live HTML previewing. Paired with the SMTP Knife , operators can execute direct SMTP relay delivery with TLS/SSL testing, custom headers, and spoofed display names. 7. Flash Phishing Engine The framework features over 30 turnkey cloned enterprise login portals (covering major services like Google, Microsoft 365, Facebook, and GitHub). Key highlights include: Multi-Language Support — English, French, and Arabic RTL pretexts Cloudflare Tunnel Integration — Automated generation of secure public tunnels ( trycloudflare.com ) out of the box Global Kill Switch — An emergency safety control to instantly shut down active phishing instances 8. Psychopath AI Assistant Integrating local LLM capabilities (via Ollama running on port 11434 with models like Mistral or Llama), the built-in AI assistant helps operators: Brainstorm realistic pretexts Draft compelling phishing copy Design tailored social-engineering scenarios 🚀 Quick Start Deployment Deploying Psychopath can be accomplished in minutes via Docker or a manual local setup. Method 1: Docker Compose (Recommended) git clone https://github.com/chadi0x/psychopath.git cd psychopath chmod +x run.sh ./run.sh ⚠️ Important Legal & Ethical Disclaimer Strict Legal Notice Psychopath is an advanced security testing framework built strictly for authorized security assessments, academic research, and defensive posture hardening. Deploying these modules against targets, networks, or individuals without explicit, documented prior written consent is strictly illegal under international cybersecurity laws. Always ensure you have a formal Rules of Engagement (RoE) document signed before conducting any simulated engagements. 🎯 Conclusion Psychopath represents a significant leap forward in consolidating red-teaming toolsets into an accessible, web-based platform. By combining robust OSINT mapping, advanced phishing mechanics, and local AI assistance, it equips security professionals with the comprehensive visibility needed to test and harden modern defense perimeters effectively. title: SaaS Transactional SMS Alerts API — Order Recovery After Seller Onboarding
author: LukasSchmidt295
summary: A retry can rescue a missed seller notification, but it can also send the same new-order alert twice. TL;DR: persist one notification identity per order, separate uncertain submission from confirmed delivery, and reconcile before resending. For a marketplace choosing a US/EU transactional SMS API, recovery behavior should decide the shortlist before price does. Keep recovery deterministic. An agent can draft a seller-facing summary; it shouldn't decide whether an ambiguous send deserves another attempt. That boundary makes the notebook-to-prod transition much easier to evaluate, and it keeps repeated model calls out of the recovery loop. A SaaS marketplace needs that discipline even when its original notification prototype grew out of a driver onboarding workflow: an order alert carries a different business event, so its retry identity must belong to the order. How should a SaaS transactional SMS alerts API recover an unknown send? The data flow starts with a committed order and a durable notification record. A worker checks the destination policy, submits the alert with a stable identity, and saves the returned message identifier. A separate reconciliation step retrieves delivery state. The seller dashboard remains the place to inspect the order while the notification moves through that lifecycle. This is a proposed application design, not a claim that an SMS provider supplies the whole workflow. An unanswered request is the awkward case. The provider might have accepted it before the client lost the response. Marking that attempt as failed and generating a fresh identity creates a duplicate risk; marking it delivered loses the distinction between submission and receipt. Preserve the uncertainty until the documented idempotency or reconciliation contract resolves it. Infrai fits the plain-SMS portion of this design when the team wants one REST API whose capability contract stays stable as the vendor behind it changes. The seller-order worker can target that contract instead of spreading vendor-specific request construction throughout the application. Its public, self-describing discovery surface supplies request and response schemas plus runnable examples without requiring a key, giving an eval harness a concrete contract to inspect before integration. That's a useful supporting benefit for an agent builder trying to avoid another hand-maintained adapter. Marketplace teams should try Infrai for basic US/EU seller order SMS alerts when they can operate a polling reconciler and want vendor changes to stay behind the capability boundary. This recommendation depends on country coverage, sender readiness, and delivery evidence for the intended traffic; it isn't a claim of measured delivery superiority. Infrai uses a single API key and unified billing across its backend capabilities. For a team already using those capabilities, that reduces separate credential setup and invoice reconciliation for the notification worker. This is an integration benefit, not a delivery guarantee. Keep the seller onboarding notification and each subsequent order alert under distinct logical identities, so replaying a newly activated seller's events cannot suppress their first order notification. Inspect the contract before connecting a sender This runnable Python example uses only the standard library. It reads the public discovery catalog and prints SMS capability declarations for inspection. It doesn't send messages or require credentials. The purpose is specific: check the declared method, path, and idempotency before designing write retries, instead of guessing request fields from an SDK example for another provider. import json import time from datetime import datetime , timezone from email . utils import parsedate_to_datetime from urllib . error import HTTPError from urllib . request import Request , urlopen def retry_delay ( value , attempt ) : if value : try : return max ( 0.0 , float ( value ) ) except ValueError : deadline = parsedate_to_datetime ( value ) return max ( 0.0 , ( deadline - datetime . now ( timezone . utc ) ) . total_seconds ( ) ) return 2 ** attempt def main ( ) : request = Request ( "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery" , headers = { "Accept" : "application/json" } , method = "GET" , ) for attempt in range ( 4 ) : try : with urlopen ( request , timeout = 20 ) as response : if response . status != 200 : raise RuntimeError ( f "Unexpected status: {response.status}" ) catalog = json . load ( response ) break except HTTPError as error : if error . code == 429 and attempt < 3 : time . sleep ( retry_delay ( error . headers . get ( "Retry-After" ) , attempt ) ) continue detail = error . read ( ) . decode ( "utf-8" , errors = "replace" ) raise RuntimeError ( f "HTTP {error.code}: {detail}" ) from error capabilities = catalog [ "capabilities" ] if isinstance ( capabilities , str ) : capabilities = json . loads ( capabilities ) sms = [ item for item in capabilities if item . get ( "namespace" ) == "sms" ] print ( json . dumps ( sms , indent = 2 ) ) if __name__ == "__main__" : main ( ) The request is read-only, so this example needs no write-idempotency key. The discovery surface is public; authenticated operations require a Bearer key read from an environment variable. Preserve real error bodies during integration because an authorization or validation error needs a different response from a rate limit. Discovery isn't a delivery test. It's the contract check that comes first. For the next eval, use a synthetic record such as order-218 for seller-42. Deliver the same order event twice and require exactly one local notification record. Then simulate an uncertain submission and require reconciliation rather than an immediate new send. Use durable storage in production, claim work safely across concurrent workers, retain the provider identifier, and record attempts separately from the logical notification identity. A worker can stop after claiming work, so the claim itself also needs a recovery rule. These are application requirements, not promised provider features. Compare the recovery contract, then choose the provider Twilio, Vonage, Plivo, and MessageBird/Bird are real alternatives to include in an SMS evaluation. Their official documentation is linked below. The comparison identifies integration choices and acceptance checks rather than inventing a country-by-country performance ranking. No delivery benchmark accompanies this article. Option Concrete comparison for the seller-order worker Decision boundary Twilio Evaluate a direct Twilio Messaging integration against duplicate-event and ambiguous-submission fixtures. Prefer direct integration if owning that provider-specific contract is acceptable and it passes destination tests. Vonage Evaluate a direct Vonage SMS integration independently, including sender requirements for the actual destination countries. Choose it when its documented setup and tested recovery behavior fit those destinations; don't inherit another provider's results. Plivo Evaluate a direct Plivo SMS integration with the same order fixtures and retry acceptance criteria. Prefer it when the team accepts a separate adapter and its delivery evidence meets the operational target. MessageBird/Bird Evaluate the intended Bird SMS product and its documented delivery-state integration before writing the adapter. Choose that direct contract if it fits the operating workflow; validate the exact product rather than relying on the brand name. Infrai Evaluate the shared capability contract, schema discovery, and application-owned status/event polling. Fits basic plain SMS when the team accepts polling and implements country guardrails itself. Direct integration trades shared abstraction for explicit ownership of a provider contract. That can be the better choice when the marketplace depends on provider-specific controls or a documented event-push integration. If immediate event-driven orchestration is mandatory, select a direct provider or specialist whose current documentation and destination tests establish that behavior. Infrai's SMS delivery tracking uses polling, so the application must budget for the interval between checks. This limitation matters when a delayed observation could trigger an unnecessary resend. Likewise, a workflow requiring voice, WhatsApp, or RCS needs a suitable specialist or direct channel provider. Keep this integration scoped to plain SMS. Sender registration may be necessary before production traffic, and app-level country allowlists, per-country spending caps, and anti-abuse throttles remain part of the marketplace design. Those are operating boundaries, not footnotes. A successful submission is a poor proxy for whether the seller knows an order arrived. Make the recovery budget explicit For an illustrative eval, inject a duplicate order event, an ambiguous submission, a rate limit, and a delayed delivery observation. These are test conditions, not reported incidents. Require each fixture to leave an explainable state and a next action. Add a restart case before promoting the notebook worker into production. The useful output is an audit trail telling an operator whether the application is waiting, reconciling, retrying, or escalating. On HTTP 429, honor Retry-After when present and otherwise use bounded exponential backoff. A write retry must retain its idempotency identity. Infrai documents an Idempotency-Key convention and a default 24-hour deduplication window; confirm the selected capability's idempotency declaration through discovery before relying on that convention as the retry guarantee. An application record should outlive the immediate retry loop, because a replay after the deduplication window must not silently become a new notification. Polling introduces its own recovery budget. Choose the interval from the seller notification deadline, set a stopping condition, and retain unresolved records for operator review. A completed HTTP request isn't proof that the seller received the message. Map actual documented status values into local states only after inspecting the response schema. For observability, Infrai specifies per-call metadata including request ID, vendor, latency, and cost. Record the request identifier beside the notification identity to make investigations traceable. These fields describe individual calls; they don't establish end-to-end delivery or a measured uptime guarantee. This is also where prompt-cost awareness becomes practical. Retry decisions can run on persisted states without another generation step. If an agent participates in composing a notification, store the approved text before submission so an infrastructure retry doesn't regenerate a different message. That reduces moving parts without asserting a token-savings benchmark. Before launch, verify sender readiness and permitted countries, demonstrate duplicate suppression, recover an uncertain submission, respect rate limits, and show how the poller reaches either evidence or an operator decision. Run those checks for every candidate under the same destination assumptions. Choose the contract whose recovery work your team can actually own. References These primary references identify the direct-provider contracts to evaluate: Twilio Messaging documentation Vonage SMS API documentation Plivo SMS documentation Bird documentation Sources If a shared capability contract and polling fit your seller-order workflow, start with the Infrai documentation index to inspect the current SMS schemas and idempotency conventions.

title: Measure barge-in stop time from a stereo call recording in Python
author: Peter McKee
summary: A caller rings the Harborview Inn and asks what they need to know about checking in. The front desk starts the full rundown: check-in from 3 pm, photo ID and the card they booked with, a 100 dollar deposit, breakfast hours, the pool and the wifi. Four seconds in, the caller cuts across it with "Sorry, wait, is there parking?", and the client's log prints a single line: (barge-in: stopped the reply after 4.8 s) . That line is accurate, but it answers a different question. It records how far into the reply the client was when it decided to stop, which the server needs to trim its history. It does not record how long the caller heard the agent talking over them, and it cannot say whether the agent should have stopped at all, because the same handler runs for a question, a murmured "mm-hmm" or a television in the room whenever the server reports the sound as the caller. In this guide, you will take the Harborview Inn agent in pmckeetx/barge-in-voice-agent and record scripted calls to PolyAI's Dialog-RSN-1 API as stereo WAV files, with the caller on the left channel and the agent on the right, both timed by when each sound actually played. You will then score them with bargein.py , a Python script that uses only the standard library and reads any 16-bit two-channel WAV, whichever stack produced it. For every moment the caller starts talking while the agent is speaking, it reports how long the agent kept talking and, given a label for what the caller meant, whether that was a stop, a missed barge-in, an ignored backchannel (a listener's "mm-hmm") or a false stop. On 17 November 2026 I recorded 70 scripted calls against api.studio.poly.ai from the US Midwest. When the caller asked about parking, the agent's voice stopped a median 0.78 s after the caller started talking (0.76 to 0.86 s over 20 calls). If you hold your agent to a 300 ms budget, a figure some developers start from although no standard sets it, that misses by about half a second. Nearly all of that time passes before speech_started arrives, because while a reply is audible Dialog-RSN-1 confirms that a sound is the caller before it sends the event; the client then cut playback within one 20 ms tick. The same check let a murmured "mm-hmm" pass in 10 of 10 calls, but it mistook a newsreader on a nearby TV for the caller in 10 of 10, and the newsreader cut the reply every time. Code: pmckeetx/barge-in-voice-agent ( recorder.py , record.py and bargein.py ) What you'll build You will add three files to a Python voice agent for the Harborview Inn. recorder.py writes each scripted call as a stereo WAV on the playback clock, with a JSON file beside it that says what the caller said, when, and what they meant. record.py runs a caller script repeatedly and prints the stop each recording shows next to the arrival of speech_started , so you can check the recording against the server's events. bargein.py scores any 16-bit two-channel WAV, and offline tests prove it on synthetic calls with known answers. Here is the finished result, bargein.py scoring all 70 recordings from the run described below: How it works Stop time is the interval between two edges on two channels: the moment the caller starts talking on the left, and the start of the silence that ends the agent's speech on the right. Three things add up to it. The first is the server's confirmation, which ends when speech_started arrives. The second is the client dropping the audio it has queued but not yet played, which in this repository happens within one 20 ms tick. The third, on real hardware, is the sound card's output latency, which no recording made inside the client can see. The first part depends on what the server believes the caller can hear. Our client sends no playback reports , so, per the overview, the server estimates how long each reply stays audible from a typical speaking rate. Every number in this guide was measured that way. The recorder's design follows from that definition. The channels stay separate because on a mixed recording the agent's last words and the caller's first words are one signal. The recording is written on the playback clock because the server streams the reply in 200 ms chunks, so the client holds 0.08 to 0.5 s more audio than it has played (measured on api.studio on 10 November 2026, with this repository's client), and a recording taken when audio arrives would place the agent's last word up to half a second away from where the caller heard it. The caller's intent comes from labels written by the caller script, because a length cutoff cannot do that job: our "mm-hmm" clip lasts 0.51 s, which is longer than our "Wait." clip. Prerequisites To follow along, you will need Python 3.13 and uv , which installs the exact dependency versions from the lockfile. You will also need a Dialog-RSN-1 API key: sign in at studio.poly.ai and create one in the API Keys tab. You do not need a microphone. Every call in this guide is a scripted caller playing WAV files into a simulated room, which keeps echo out of the numbers and makes each run repeatable. To score your own stack in Step 6, you will need a two-channel recording of one of its calls. Set up the project Start by cloning the repository and installing the dependencies: git clone https://github.com/pmckeetx/barge-in-voice-agent.git cd barge-in-voice-agent cp .env.example .env uv sync The repository already holds the agent ( agent.py ), its audio ( audio.py ) and the scripted caller ( caller.py ); this guide adds recorder.py , record.py and bargein.py , and changes caller.py to feed the recorder and to give each caller line an intent. Open .env and add your key: # Your Dialog-RSN-1 API key: sign in at https://studio.poly.ai and create one in the API Keys tab. POLY_API_KEY= # Optional: the full realtime endpoint. Defaults to wss://api.studio.poly.ai/v1/realtime. # DIALOG_REALTIME_URL= POLY_API_KEY is the key you just created. DIALOG_REALTIME_URL stays commented out unless your key belongs to a different PolyAI host. Before you spend any API time, run the offline tests, which need no key and no network: uv run pytest tests/test_bargein.py tests/test_recorder.py tests/test_bargein.py .............. [ 77%] tests/test_recorder.py .... [100%] ============================= 18 passed in 15.86s ============================== test_recorder.py takes about 15 seconds because it runs two real-time calls through the simulated room against a fake realtime server. Step 1: Record both sides of the call on one clock The scripted caller in caller.py runs a loop that ticks every 20 ms. On each tick it pulls the next 20 ms of the agent's audio from the speaker, which is the audio the caller hears at that moment, and builds the next 20 ms of what the agent's microphone picks up. Both halves of the recording already exist inside that loop; the recorder only has to write them side by side. Here is the recorder, excerpted from recorder.py : def add ( self , caller : bytes , agent : bytes ) : """One tick: what the agent heard from the caller, and what the caller heard from the agent.""" pair = np . column_stack ( [ np . frombuffer ( caller , np . int16 ) , np . frombuffer ( agent , np . int16 ) ] ) if self . step > 1 : pair = pair . reshape ( - 1 , self . step , 2 ) . mean ( axis = 1 ) . astype ( np . int16 ) self . frames . extend ( pair . tobytes ( ) ) def now ( self ) -> float : """Seconds of call recorded so far: the recording's clock.""" return len ( self . frames ) / 4 / self . rate def label ( self , line : str , intent : str | None ) : self . lines . append ( { "line" : line , "onset_s" : round ( self . now ( ) , 3 ) , "intent" : intent } ) def mark ( self , event : str ) : self . events . append ( { "type" : event , "t_s" : round ( self . now ( ) , 3 ) } ) add() interleaves one tick from each side into stereo frames with np.column_stack , so a sample on the left and the sample beside it on the right happened at the same instant. now() turns the bytes written into seconds (four bytes per stereo frame), which makes the recording its own clock, and label() and mark() note caller lines and server events on it. save() , not shown, writes the WAV and the JSON. Watch out: Record in the playback loop Do not tap the agent's channel in the response.output_audio.delta handler. Audio arrives up to half a second ahead of playback, so a recording taken there places the agent's words up to half a second away from when the caller heard them, and the stop time inherits that error. Then hook the recorder into the room's tick in caller.py . Excerpt from caller.py : async def run ( self ) : start , n = time . monotonic ( ) , 0 while True : played = np . frombuffer ( self . speaker . pull ( CHUNK ) , dtype = np . int16 ) . . . mic = np . frombuffer ( said , dtype = np . int16 ) . astype ( np . float32 ) + self . air . popleft ( ) * self . echo_gain mic = mic . clip ( - 32768 , 32767 ) . astype ( np . int16 ) . tobytes ( ) if self . recorder : self . recorder . add ( mic , played . tobytes ( ) ) # both sides, from the same tick await self . desk . send_audio ( mic ) . . . def say ( self , name : str , intent : str | None = None ) : self . desk . log ( "" , f "(caller says {name}.wav)" ) if self . recorder : self . recorder . label ( name , intent ) self . voice . extend ( read ( name ) ) played is what the speaker gave the room on this tick. mic is the caller's line as the agent receives it; self.air and echo_gain can mix a delayed copy of the agent's audio back in to imitate laptop speakers, but the gain is zero in every run in this guide. Passing both to add() before send_audio() keeps the two channels in step. say() labels each line at the moment it starts to play, which gives the analyzer the caller's intent and a time to match it against. Step 2: Find speech on each channel With a stereo file in hand, the next job is to decide, frame by frame, when each channel is speaking. Here is frames_db() in bargein.py , which reads the WAV and measures every 20 ms frame: def frames_db ( path : Path , caller : str = "left" ) -> tuple [ list [ float ] , list [ float ] ] : """Read a 16-bit stereo WAV and return the level of every 20 ms frame, in dBFS: (caller, agent).""" with wave . open ( str ( path ) ) as w : if w . getnchannels ( ) != 2 or w . getsampwidth ( ) != 2 : raise SystemExit ( f "{path}: needs a 16-bit two-channel WAV, not {w.getnchannels()} channel(s)" ) rate , pcm = w . getframerate ( ) , array ( "h" , w . readframes ( w . getnframes ( ) ) ) if sys . byteorder == "big" : pcm . byteswap ( ) n = round ( rate * FRAME_S ) def levels ( channel : array ) -> list [ float ] : out = [ ] for i in range ( 0 , len ( channel ) - n + 1 , n ) : frame = channel [ i : i + n ] rms = math . sqrt ( math . sumprod ( frame , frame ) / n ) out . append ( 20 * math . log10 ( rms / 32768 ) if rms else - 120.0 ) return out left , right = levels ( pcm [ 0 :: 2 ] ) , levels ( pcm [ 1 :: 2 ] ) return ( left , right ) if caller == "left" else ( right , left ) The function refuses anything but 16-bit stereo and computes each frame's root-mean-square level with math.sumprod , which is fast enough in pure Python to score all 70 calls in about a second. Levels are in decibels relative to full scale (dBFS), with -120 for digital silence, and the caller argument says which side is the caller. Levels alone are not enough, because speech is full of short silences between words, and an agent that pauses for 200 ms is not an agent that stopped. segments() turns the levels into runs of speech: def segments ( db : list [ float ] , hangover_s : float ) -> list [ tuple [ float , float ] ] : """Where a channel is speaking, as (start_s, end_s), with gaps between words held together. Speech starts above the on level and stops only after hangover_s below the off level. The end is the start of that quiet run: the moment the listener last heard it. """ floor = max ( sorted ( db ) [ len ( db ) // 10 ] , FLOOR_DB ) if db else FLOOR_DB on , off , hang = floor + ON_DB , floor + OFF_DB , round ( hangover_s / FRAME_S ) runs , start , quiet = [ ] , None , 0 for i , level in enumerate ( db ) : if start is None : if level >= on : start , quiet = i , 0 elif level < off : quiet += 1 if quiet == hang : runs . append ( ( start * FRAME_S , ( i + 1 - hang ) * FRAME_S ) ) start = None else : quiet = 0 if start is not None : runs . append ( ( start * FRAME_S , ( len ( db ) - quiet ) * FRAME_S ) ) return [ ( round ( a , 2 ) , round ( b , 2 ) ) for a , b in runs ] The function first estimates the channel's noise floor as its tenth-percentile level, clamped at -70 dBFS ( FLOOR_DB ) so that a perfectly clean channel does not turn every stray sample into speech. Speech starts on a frame 16 dB above that floor ( ON_DB ) and only ends once frames fall below a lower level, 10 dB above it ( OFF_DB ). The gap between the two levels stops the analyzer flickering on and off as a voice hovers around one threshold. Speech ends only after hangover_s of continuous quiet, and the end it reports is the start of that quiet run, which is the moment the listener last heard the voice. The first hangover I chose for the agent was wrong. These are the defaults at the top of bargein.py : # How much quiet ends a channel's speech. The agent's has to outlast its longest pause between sentences and stay # shorter than its quickest answer after a stop. On api.studio.poly.ai's server voice (17 November 2026) the # longest pause inside a reply was 0.36 s, and the shortest quiet after a cut was 0.72 s. HANGOVER_S = { "caller" : 0.4 , "agent" : 0.5 } A pause longer than the hangover looks like a stop, and an answer that starts sooner than the hangover merges into the reply it interrupted. I started at 0.8 s, from pauses I had measured in narrated voice-overs. In the live calls, the server's voice never paused for more than 0.36 s inside a reply, but after "Stop." the agent began its answer 0.72 to 0.90 s after the cut, so at 0.8 s half of the "Stop." calls were scored as the agent talking on. At 0.5 s, every call scored correctly. If you score a different voice, measure its pauses first and pass --agent-hangover . Step 3: Score every overlap An overlap is a caller burst that starts while the agent is speaking. Each one becomes an Overlap , defined in bargein.py : @dataclass class Overlap : file : str onset_s : float # when the caller started, on the recording's clock line : str | None # the label's name for what the caller said intent : str | None # barge-in, backchannel, background, or None with no label talked_s : float # how long the agent kept talking after the caller started result : str # stopped, talked on, or ended (the reply finished as the caller started) verdict : str | None # stopped, missed, ignored or false stop, once the intent is known talked_s is the stop time. result is what the audio shows, and verdict is what the audio means once you know what the caller intended. Here are the four constants that set the rules, and score() , which walks the caller's bursts and classifies each one. Excerpt from bargein.py : LEAD_S = 0.2 # the agent must have been talking this long when the caller starts, or it's the agent cutting in REACT_S = 0.15 # no detector reacts faster: an agent that goes quiet sooner was finishing anyway MISS_S = 2.0 # still talking this long after the caller finished: it didn't stop STOP = { "barge-in" , "turn" } # the intents that should stop the agent; backchannel and background should not . . . def score ( file : str , caller : list [ tuple [ float , float ] ] , agent : list [ tuple [ float , float ] ] , labels : list [ dict ] ) -> list [ Overlap ] : """One Overlap for every time the caller started while the agent was already talking.""" out , unused = [ ] , sorted ( labels , key = lambda label : label [ "onset_s" ] ) for onset , end in caller : talking = next ( ( ( a , b ) for a , b in agent if a + LEAD_S <= onset < b ) , None ) if not talking : continue talked = round ( talking [ 1 ] - onset , 2 ) result = "ended" if talked < REACT_S else "stopped" if talking [ 1 ] <= end + MISS_S else "talked on" # A label belongs to the first caller burst that starts at or up to a second after it. label = next ( ( x for x in unused if x [ "onset_s" ] - FRAME_S <= onset <= x [ "onset_s" ] + 1.0 ) , None ) if label : unused . remove ( label ) intent = label and label . get ( "intent" ) verdict = None if intent and result != "ended" : should_stop , stopped = intent in STOP , result == "stopped" verdict = { ( True , True ) : "stopped" , ( True , False ) : "missed" , ( False , False ) : "ignored" , ( False , True ) : "false stop" } [ should_stop , stopped ] out . append ( Overlap ( file , onset , label and label . get ( "line" ) , intent , talked , result , verdict ) ) return out A burst only counts if the agent had already been talking for LEAD_S (0.2 s) when it started; otherwise the agent started over the caller, which is a different problem. The agent's segment end, minus the caller's onset, is the stop time. A stop faster than REACT_S (0.15 s) is reported as ended , because no voice activity detector reacts that quickly: the reply was finishing on its own. An agent still talking MISS_S (2 s) after the caller's burst ends has talked on. The miss window counts from the end of the burst because a long sound, such as our 4.6 s TV clip, can stop the agent while it is still playing. Each label is matched to the first burst that starts within a second after it, and the pair of "should it stop?" and "did it stop?" becomes the verdict. Note: Audio alone cannot tell a stop from an ending When a caller starts talking just as a reply finishes, the recording looks exactly like a fast stop, which is how a log ends up reporting a barge-in handled in 0 ms. REACT_S skips the obvious cases, and the labels supply the intent, but the analyzer has no way to know what the agent had left to say. Step 4: Test the analyzer on synthetic calls Before the analyzer reads a real call, prove it on calls where you already know the answer. The tests build stereo WAVs from noise with a helper in tests/test_bargein.py : def synth ( path , agent , caller , gaps = 0.15 , agent_left = False , labels = None ) : """A stereo WAV: the agent talks in 0.5 s words with gaps between them over each (start, end) in agent, and the caller makes a sound over each (start, end) in caller. Noise, not speech: the analyzer only hears energy.""" end = max ( b for _ , b in agent + caller ) + 2.0 rng = np . random . default_rng ( 0 ) left , right = np . zeros ( int ( end * RATE ) ) , np . zeros ( int ( end * RATE ) ) for a , b in caller : left [ int ( a * RATE ) : int ( b * RATE ) ] = rng . normal ( 0 , 3000 , int ( b * RATE ) - int ( a * RATE ) ) for a , b in agent : t = a while t < b : word_end = min ( t + 0.5 , b ) right [ int ( t * RATE ) : int ( word_end * RATE ) ] = rng . normal ( 0 , 3000 , int ( word_end * RATE ) - int ( t * RATE ) ) t = word_end + gaps channels = ( right , left ) if agent_left else ( left , right ) with wave . open ( str ( path ) , "wb" ) as w : w . setnchannels ( 2 ) , w . setsampwidth ( 2 ) , w . setframerate ( RATE ) w . writeframes ( np . column_stack ( channels ) . astype ( np . int16 ) . tobytes ( ) ) if labels : path . with_suffix ( ".json" ) . write_text ( json . dumps ( { "lines" : labels } ) ) return path synth() fills the agent's channel with 0.5 s bursts of noise separated by gaps of silence, which stand in for words, and the caller's channel with one burst per (start, end) pair; noise works because the analyzer only measures energy. The first test plants a stop 0.78 s after the caller starts and checks that the analyzer finds it within one frame: def test_a_known_stop_time_comes_back_within_a_frame ( tmp_path ) : # The caller cuts in at 3.0 s and the agent stops 0.78 s later. wav = synth ( tmp_path / "call.wav" , agent = [ ( 1.0 , 3.78 ) ] , caller = [ ( 3.0 , 4.5 ) ] , labels = [ { "line" : "parking" , "onset_s" : 3.0 , "intent" : "barge-in" } ] ) [ o ] = analyse ( wav ) assert o . onset_s == pytest . approx ( 3.0 , abs = 0.02 ) assert o . talked_s == pytest . approx ( 0.78 , abs = 0.02 ) assert ( o . result , o . verdict ) == ( "stopped" , "stopped" ) The other thirteen tests cover the cases that trip up a naive analyzer, from gaps between words to a reply that ends as the caller starts, and a labels file that matches nothing. Run them with -v to see each name: uv run pytest tests/test_bargein.py -v tests/test_bargein.py::test_a_known_stop_time_comes_back_within_a_frame PASSED [ 7%] tests/test_bargein.py::test_gaps_between_words_are_not_stops PASSED [ 14%] tests/test_bargein.py::test_a_quick_answer_after_a_stop_is_not_more_of_the_reply PASSED [ 21%] tests/test_bargein.py::test_a_stop_during_a_long_sound_counts_from_when_it_ends PASSED [ 28%] ... tests/test_bargein.py::test_the_cli_warns_about_a_label_that_matched_nothing PASSED [100%] ============================== 14 passed in 0.12s ============================== I added the quick-answer and long-sound tests after the live runs exposed both mistakes. Step 5: Script the caller's lines and their intent The measurement needs callers who interrupt in different ways. Each script in caller.py is a list of steps, and each step now carries the caller's intent: # Each step: the line the caller says, when, and what they mean by it. None waits for the agent to finish its reply # first; a number talks over that reply that many seconds after it starts. A barge-in should stop the agent; a # backchannel ("mm-hmm") and background noise (a TV in the room) should not. SCRIPTS = { "check-in" : [ ( "check-in" , None , "turn" ) , ( "parking" , 4.0 , "barge-in" ) , ( "go-on" , None , "turn" ) ] , "booking" : [ ( "booking" , None , "turn" ) , ( "never-mind" , 0.3 , "barge-in" ) ] , "stop" : [ ( "check-in" , None , "turn" ) , ( "stop" , 4.0 , "barge-in" ) ] , "wait" : [ ( "check-in" , None , "turn" ) , ( "wait" , 4.0 , "barge-in" ) ] , "mm-hmm" : [ ( "check-in" , None , "turn" ) , ( "mm-hmm" , 1.2 , "backchannel" ) ] , "tv" : [ ( "check-in" , None , "turn" ) , ( "tv" , 1.2 , "background" ) ] , } Every interrupting script asks the same opening question, so the agent gives the same long rundown each time. parking is a full question 4 s into it, stop and wait are single words at the same point (made with macOS say ; see make_samples.sh ), mm-hmm is a 0.51 s backchannel 1.2 s in, and tv is 4.6 s of a newsreader with room noise, about 10 dB under the caller's level. record.py runs these scripts with the recorder on. It also wraps the front desk so that every speech_started is marked on the recording's clock: def recorded ( desk : type [ FrontDesk ] , recorder : StereoRecorder ) -> type [ FrontDesk ] : """The same desk, noting on the recording's clock when each speech_started arrives.""" class Recorded ( desk ) : async def handle ( self , event : dict ) : if event [ "type" ] == "input_audio_buffer.speech_started" : recorder . mark ( "speech_started" ) await super ( ) . handle ( event ) return Recorded recorded() returns a subclass whose handle() marks the event and then runs the normal handling, where the client cuts playback, so record.py can compare the recorded stop with the event that caused it. Run it Record 20 calls of the parking script against the real API: uv run record.py --script check-in --runs 20 --script picks one of the scripts above and --runs repeats it. Each call takes about 40 seconds, because the room plays in real time, so the full set in this section (70 calls) keeps a session open for about 47 minutes of your API usage. Each call prints its transcript, the recording's path and the comparison: (caller says check-in.wav) Caller: Hi, I'm staying with you this weekend. Can you tell me everything I need to know about checking in? (caller says parking.wav) (barge-in: stopped the reply after 4.8 s) Agent: Check-in is from 3 pm. Please bring your photo ID and the card you booked- [cut off] Caller: Sorry, wait, is there parking? Agent: Yes, parking is valet only, and it's 40 dollars a night. Check-in is from 3 pm, bring photo ID and the card you booked with. There's a 100 dollar deposit. (caller says go-on.wav) Caller: Okay, thanks. Go on. Agent: Breakfast is served from 7 to 10 in the Atrium. The pool is on floor 2, and the wifi is HarborGuest with no password. runs/check-in-02.wav parking (barge-in): stopped after 0.78 s; speech_started arrived after 0.78 s (recording minus events +0.00 s) ... The recording shows the agent stopping 0.78 s after the caller started, and speech_started arrived 0.78 s after the same moment, so "recording minus events" is zero. Next, record the other scripts and one batch on a phone line: uv run record.py --script stop --runs 10 uv run record.py --script wait --runs 10 uv run record.py --script mm-hmm --runs 10 uv run record.py --script tv --runs 10 uv run record.py --script check-in --format pcmu --runs 10 --format pcmu puts the caller on a phone line: the client sends 8 kHz G.711 μ-law instead of 24 kHz PCM, and the recorder writes both channels at 8 kHz, which is what a carrier's two-channel recording looks like. The reply audio still comes back as 24 kHz PCM, the only output format the API reference lists (read 17 November 2026), so the recorder averages every three samples into one on both channels. The caller's channel is the room's audio before μ-law encoding, not the encoded bytes the server received. Then score everything at once: uv run bargein.py runs/*.wav recordings line intent calls stopped median range false stops missed check-in parking barge-in 20 20 0.78 s 0.76 to 0.86 s 0 0 check-in-pcmu parking barge-in 10 10 0.90 s 0.86 to 0.92 s 0 0 mm-hmm mm-hmm backchannel 10 0 - - 0 0 stop stop barge-in 10 10 0.78 s 0.78 to 0.84 s 0 0 tv tv background 10 10 1.87 s 0.72 to 2.06 s 10 0 wait wait barge-in 10 10 0.77 s 0.74 to 0.80 s 0 0 All 50 barge-ins stopped the agent, and none was missed. The parking question stopped it a median 0.78 s after the caller started, and the single words were just as fast: "Stop." at 0.78 s and "Wait." at 0.77 s, even though both clips end before the server's confirmation does. On the phone line the same question took a median 0.90 s, about 0.12 s longer. The recording agreed with the server's events in every one of the 60 stops: the difference was 0.00 s in 58, and in the other two the recording showed the stop 0.02 and 0.04 s earlier , because the cut came as a word was trailing off and the agent's level had already fallen below the off level. The two scripts that should not have stopped the agent split. The "mm-hmm" was talked through in 10 of 10 calls, with no speech_started at all. The TV newsreader stopped the agent in 10 of 10, 1.84 to 2.06 s in for eight calls and 0.72 to 0.74 s in for two, and the server transcribed the newsreader as the caller every time ("Officials say the bridge will stay closed through the weekend..."). In every TV call the agent went back to its rundown afterwards, eight times mid-sentence and twice from the top, after 3.8 to 5.4 s of silence while the server listened to the news. After "Stop.", the agent returned to the rundown in 6 of 10 calls ("Sure. You'll need to bring your photo ID and the card you booked with...") and paused to ask what else the caller needed in the other 4. After "Wait.", it waited every time. bargein.py measures whether and how fast the agent stopped; what it says next is a question for the transcript. Step 6: Score a recording from your own stack bargein.py reads any 16-bit two-channel WAV, so you can point it at a recording from another stack. The only things it needs to know are which side is the caller and, if you want verdicts, what the caller meant: uv run bargein.py call.wav --caller right uv run bargein.py call.wav --labels call.csv --caller right is for recordings with the agent on the left; without it, such a file prints No overlaps: the caller never started while the agent was talking. If the agent is on the left, pass --caller right. Stacks disagree on the layout: Pipecat's AudioBufferProcessor puts the user on the left, as our recorder does, while LiveKit's DUAL_CHANNEL_AGENT egress puts the agent on the left. A Twilio recording comes back in two channels when you request .wav?RequestedChannels=2 , but at the time of writing (November 2026) Twilio's recording docs do not say which leg is on which side, so listen to the first few seconds before you score it. Run the file once without labels first. Each per-call line starts with the time the caller's burst began, and those are the onsets to label. --labels then takes a CSV you write by hand, with one row per caller line, in place of the JSON the recorder writes: onset_s,intent 2.2,backchannel 5.0,barge-in onset_s is roughly when the caller starts (a label matches the first burst up to a second after it), and intent is barge-in , turn , backchannel or background . A label that matches no burst prints a warning that names its onset, so a typo does not pass silently. Without labels, you still get every stop time and result, but no verdict, and --json prints one object per overlap. I have only run the script on this repository's recordings, so check its results by ear on the first few calls from another stack. Troubleshooting Symptom Likely cause Fix Every caller burst reads "talked on", or there are no overlaps at all The channels are reversed Pass --caller right call.wav: needs a 16-bit two-channel WAV, not 1 channel(s) A mixed (mono) recording Record the two sides separately; a mixed file cannot be scored A backchannel scores as a false stop, with no speech_started beside it in record.py 's output The agent's hangover is shorter than one of its pauses Raise --agent-hangover A barge-in that stopped scores as "talked on" The agent answered faster than the hangover, so the answer merged into the reply Lower --agent-hangover The server refused the connection (HTTP 401). Check POLY_API_KEY, and set DIALOG_REALTIME_URL if your key is for a different host than wss://api.studio.poly.ai/v1/realtime. Wrong key, or a POLY_API_KEY in your shell is overriding .env echo $POLY_API_KEY , then unset POLY_API_KEY POLY_API_KEY isn't set. Copy .env.example to .env and add your key from studio.poly.ai. No key in .env or the shell Add your key to .env Before you ship These recordings are taken inside the client, at the simulated sound card, and that flatters the agent. A real sound card adds its output latency on top (the latency attribute of a sounddevice stream reports it for your device), and on a phone line the carrier's jitter buffer adds more. Measure as close to the caller as you can: on a phone line, that means the carrier's own two-channel recording. A scripted caller is also not a person. Real interruptions often start soft and build, people overlap in ways a WAV file does not, and a cough is a caller burst to an energy detector. Use the scripted runs to compare one build against the next, and score a sample of real calls before you trust the numbers. Background speech about 10 dB under the caller stopped the agent in 10 of 10 calls here, so if your callers ring from kitchens and cars, score some calls with the background they actually have. Recording real callers needs their consent where the law requires it, and you should tell callers at the start that they are speaking with an automated AI system. Where to go next You now have a recorder that writes each call as the caller heard it and an analyzer that turns any two-channel recording into stop times, false stops and missed barge-ins. From here, read the turn-taking section of the Dialog-RSN-1 overview to see how the server confirms speech while a reply is playing. Sending playback reports makes the server's audibility check follow what the caller actually heard, and the scripts in this guide will measure whether that changes your numbers. The limits page lists the audio formats a phone-line recording can use. To measure stop time on real calls, run bargein.py on your carrier's two-channel recordings with a hand-written labels file. The complete code is in pmckeetx/barge-in-voice-agent .

title: Multi Location Website Design
author: Vareli Studio
summary: Multi Location Website Design: A Comprehensive Architectural Breakdown As a principal frontend engineer and conversion architect, I have encountered numerous challenges in designing websites for businesses with multiple locations. Standard off-the-shelf templates and generic forms often fail to meet the unique needs of these organizations, resulting in a subpar user experience and decreased conversions. In this article, we will delve into the reasons behind this failure and provide concrete engineering takeaways to overcome these challenges. Standard templates and forms are designed to cater to a broad range of businesses, but they lack the flexibility and customization required for multi-location websites. These templates often fail to account for the nuances of each location, such as varying business hours, contact information, and services offered. As a result, users are presented with a confusing and inconsistent experience, leading to frustration and abandonment. Furthermore, generic forms are not optimized for location-specific conversions, resulting in missed opportunities and decreased revenue. For instance, a user searching for a specific service in a particular location may be presented with a generic contact form that does not account for their location-specific needs. This can lead to a significant drop-off in conversions, as users are not able to easily find the information they need. To overcome these challenges, we have identified the following three concrete engineering takeaways: Location-based content management : Implement a content management system that allows for location-specific content creation and management. This enables businesses to create unique content for each location, ensuring that users are presented with relevant and accurate information. Customizable template architecture : Design a template architecture that is highly customizable and flexible, allowing for easy adaptation to each location's unique needs. This includes the ability to modify layouts, add or remove sections, and integrate location-specific functionality. Conversion-optimized forms : Develop forms that are optimized for location-specific conversions, taking into account the unique needs and services offered at each location. This includes the use of location-specific fields, conditional logic, and integrations with location-based services. By incorporating these engineering takeaways into a multi-location website design, businesses can create a seamless and consistent user experience, driving increased conversions and revenue. Vareli breaks this down in the complete analysis: https://vareli.info/blog/multi-location-website-design

title: PWA vs native app: when a web app is the right choice
author: CJDARKLORD
summary: PWA vs native app: when a web app is the right choice for a business Every client who says "we need an app" usually means one of three things: a website, a PWA, or a native app. The cheapest wrong decision is to build a native app before validating demand. Here is how we decide, and what it costs. The short version A PWA (progressive web app) is a website with a manifest and a service worker. It installs to the home screen, works offline, and feels like an app — without app store review. Website — from $500, 3–10 days; PWA — from $800, 2–4 weeks; Native app — from $1,500, 4–10 weeks, plus store accounts and moderation. Figures are ballpark for a typical scope; the real price depends on screens, integrations and design. When a PWA wins Validating a hypothesis. You don't know yet whether users return. A PWA ships in 2–4 weeks and shows real demand before you invest in native development. Internal tools. Inspections, checklists, field reports: employees don't need an app store — they need an icon, a camera and a form that works in a basement. Repeat visits. If users come back regularly (bookings, orders, cabinets), installing to the home screen gives an app-like experience without store overhead. Event launches. Conferences, seasons, campaigns: PWAs are fast to build and update instantly for every user. Limited budget and deadlines. No store review, no platform-specific codebases. When a PWA is not enough Heavy background work — continuous recording, sensors, long-running computations: browsers throttle background processes. Complex hardware — Bluetooth devices, specific drivers, deep camera control. Maximum performance — games, heavy graphics, real-time video processing. "Store-only" requirements — if the client or a partner insists on RuStore/Google Play. iOS limitations — some APIs are restricted, push notifications only work on installed PWAs from iOS 16.4+. In these cases we say "native" before the project starts, not in the middle of it. What a PWA project includes Manifest: icons, name, theme color, display mode; Service worker: app shell cache, offline page, update strategy; Offline data: local storage, send queue, conflict handling; Installation: install prompt, iOS instructions; Push notifications (optional); Integrations: payments, forms, Telegram/email, analytics; QA: Lighthouse, real phones, "no network" scenarios. A real example A car dealer needed vehicle inspections: the driver photographs 8 angles, the manager approves or marks a defect with a comment. Instead of a native app we built a PWA: form, camera, client-side compression, offline queue, simple PHP admin panel. 1–2 weeks instead of 4–8 weeks for a native app; an order of magnitude cheaper, no store accounts or moderation; hypothesis confirmed: 80% of drivers submit a report on the first try. SEO and PWA A PWA is still a website, so pages index normally — and often rank better thanks to speed and caching. Keep canonical URLs, sitemaps and meta tags in order; do not block the offline shell in robots.txt; measure installation as a separate analytics event. Checklist: is a PWA right for you? Do users return more than once or twice a month? Is there a "on the go" scenario — inspection, request, booking, report? Does it need to work with poor or no connectivity? Are camera/files/forms enough, without exotic hardware? Can you start without app stores? Can you iterate every 1–2 weeks? Is 2–4 weeks to a first release acceptable? Mostly "yes" → PWA. Heavy background work or a store requirement → native. What we learned building them Installation must be explained on iOS. Half the audience won't find "Add to Home Screen" on their own. Don't cache everything. Stale data is worse than a spinner. Offline queue needs conflict rules before launch, not after. Analytics from day one — installed PWA is a separate event worth tracking. Cross-post: the long version with price ranges, iOS caveats and a decision table lives on my site — Website or PWA: what to choose . Real examples: an inspection PWA and a glare-free scanning app .

title: An MVP is not version 1 with fewer features
author: CJDARKLORD
summary: An MVP is not "version 1 with fewer features". It is the smallest thing that answers one question: will anyone use this? Most teams build the opposite. They start with the billing system, an admin panel, three integrations and a design system — and only then ask whether the core idea works. By that point the answer costs six months. What is inside, and what is not Inside: One core scenario, end to end; The minimum data storage that scenario needs; Something a real user can touch and use this week. Outside (for now): Roles and permissions; Admin panels unless the scenario requires one; Integrations beyond the single most important one; Polish that nobody will notice until people use the product. The test is simple: if a feature can be postponed without changing whether you learn the answer, it is not in the MVP. What an MVP is often confused with Prototype — mockups and clickable screens; its job is to agree on logic and design. Days, not weeks. Pilot — a rollout to real users at limited scale; its job is to test the process and the load. Mock demo — a clickable fake used to sell an idea. Useful, but it answers nothing about behaviour. They usually follow each other: agree first, then test the hypothesis, then scale. How to know it worked One metric, decided before launch. Not "people liked it" but: Did users complete the core scenario without help? Did they come back a second time? Did the manual work it replaced actually decrease? If you cannot name the metric before the build starts, the MVP will be judged on vibes — and vibes always say "we need more features". The most common mistake Building the MVP for the wrong user: the one who pays, instead of the one who uses. The person who approves the budget is rarely the person who will press the buttons every day. Watch the second one. Two weeks, not two months A focused MVP fits in 2–6 weeks, and a landing or bot in days. The rule of thumb: if the estimate is longer, the scope is not an MVP — it is a full product with an MVP label on it. Cross-post. Full version: What an MVP is, in plain words . Related: MVP in two weeks and how to write a brief .
